topic: Lactate, Perfusion & Resuscitation Targets — Chasing the Right Number
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Critical Care Unit
speakerBio: A physiologist-intensivist who teaches that the most dangerous number in sepsis is the one you chase without understanding — and that the fingertip often beats the blood gas.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

Your septic patient's lactate came back at 5.0. You give fluid; two hours later it is 4.4. The nurse asks: "Do we keep pushing fluid until it's normal?" It is the most seductive trap in sepsis resuscitation — chasing a number to zero. This session is about what lactate actually means, why it rises for reasons that have nothing to do with oxygen, and which target — lactate clearance, capillary refill, venous oxygen saturation, or MAP — you should actually resuscitate to.

1 · What is lactate really telling you? 🧪

Lactate is the end-product of anaerobic glycolysis — but that is only half the story, and the half that misleads. There are two mechanistic types:

Type A — hypoxicType B — non-hypoxic
MechanismTissue oxygen delivery fails → pyruvate cannot enter oxidative phosphorylation → shunted to lactateLactate rises without tissue hypoxia — altered metabolism or reduced clearance
Causes in sepsisHypoperfusion, shock, severe anaemia/hypoxaemia, regional ischaemia (dead gut)Adrenergic β₂-driven aerobic glycolysis (endogenous stress catecholamines and your adrenaline/salbutamol), impaired hepatic clearance, mitochondrial dysfunction, thiamine deficiency

In septic shock the early rise is largely Type A — a genuine marker of hypoperfusion and a strong, dose-dependent predictor of death (a lactate >4 mmol/L is one of the defining thresholds of septic shock, alongside vasopressor-dependent hypotension). But as resuscitation proceeds, a persistently elevated lactate may be increasingly Type B — driven by the very catecholamines you are infusing and by sluggish hepatic clearance, not ongoing under-resuscitation.

💡 One-liner

A high lactate is a smoke alarm, not a fuel gauge. It tells you something is burning; it does not tell you the tank is empty. Do not pour fluid at a number that adrenaline is generating.

2 · The mechanism trap — why chasing lactate can drown a patient 🌊

  1. Early sepsis: lactate 5.0, mostly hypoperfusion (Type A). Fluid + pressors improve flow → lactate falls to 3.
  2. Now the patient is adequately filled, on noradrenaline, with a normal MAP and warm peripheries — but lactate sits at 2.5 and will not fully normalise.
  3. That residual lactate is now largely Type B: β₂-adrenergic aerobic glycolysis (endogenous stress hormones plus your catecholamine infusion) and reduced hepatic clearance.
  4. If you interpret it as persistent hypoperfusion and keep giving fluid, you drive the patient into fluid overload — pulmonary oedema, worse gas exchange, abdominal and tissue oedema, higher mortality.

This is why the target is lactate CLEARANCE (a downward trend), not lactate normalisation to zero, and why we increasingly cross-check lactate against a direct measure of peripheral perfusion.

3 · Lactate clearance as a resuscitation target 📉

SSC 2021 suggests guiding resuscitation to decrease lactate in patients with an elevated lactate, as a marker of tissue hypoperfusion — over serial measurements rather than a single value.

  • A commonly cited goal is a ≥10–20% fall over the first 2 hours, and trending it every 2–4 hours during active resuscitation.
  • Jones 2010 showed that resuscitating to lactate clearance was non-inferior to targeting central venous oxygen saturation (ScvO₂) — lactate clearance is an easier, cheaper surrogate for the same physiological goal.
  • Failure to clear lactate despite resuscitation is an ominous sign — it should prompt a hunt for an uncontrolled source (Session 6), ongoing hypoperfusion, or a Type B cause, not simply more fluid.

4 · Capillary refill time — resuscitating to the fingertip 👆

Capillary refill time (CRT) is a direct, zero-cost bedside marker of peripheral perfusion: press the fingertip/nail bed for a few seconds and time the return of colour; >3 seconds is abnormal. It reflects the microcirculation you are actually trying to restore.

🎯 Contrast — lactate clearance vs CRT-guided resuscitation (ANDROMEDA-SHOCK)

The ANDROMEDA-SHOCK trial randomised septic shock patients to resuscitation targeting CRT normalisation (every 30 min) versus lactate clearance. The CRT-guided arm had no worse 28-day mortality (a strong trend toward lower mortality that missed statistical significance), less organ dysfunction at 72 h, and — importantly — patients received less fluid. A subsequent Bayesian re-analysis suggested a high probability of benefit. Take-away: CRT is at least non-inferior to lactate clearance, avoids the Type-B lactate trap, and pushes you to give less fluid. Peripheral perfusion at the fingertip is a legitimate — arguably better — endpoint than the lactate number.

💡 Pearl

A normalising CRT with a warm, well-perfused patient trumps a stubbornly 'high' lactate. If the fingertip refills fast and the patient looks perfused, that residual lactate is probably Type B — stop chasing it with fluid.

5 · Venous oxygen saturation — the extraction readout 🩸

Mixed venous (SvO₂, pulmonary artery) or central venous (ScvO₂, SVC) oxygen saturation reflects the balance between oxygen delivery and tissue extraction.

  • Low ScvO₂ (<70%): delivery is failing to meet demand — inadequate cardiac output, anaemia, or hypoxaemia. It argues for improving flow (fluid if fluid-responsive, an inotrope, or transfusion).
  • High/normal ScvO₂ in a sick septic patient: can be falsely reassuring — mitochondrial dysfunction and microcirculatory shunting mean the tissues cannot extract the oxygen, so the venous blood stays saturated despite tissue distress. A high ScvO₂ does not prove adequate perfusion.

6 · The rise and fall of protocolised EGDT 📚

Rivers 2001 introduced Early Goal-Directed Therapy (EGDT): a rigid protocol in the first 6 hours targeting CVP 8–12, MAP ≥65, urine output, and ScvO₂ ≥70% (using fluids, pressors, transfusion to Hct ≥30%, and dobutamine). His single-centre trial showed a dramatic mortality reduction and reshaped a generation of sepsis care.

TrialFinding
Rivers 2001 (single centre)Protocolised EGDT → large mortality benefit vs the usual care of its era
ProCESS (USA)Protocolised EGDT no better than protocol-based standard care or usual care
ARISE (Australasia)EGDT no mortality benefit over usual care
ProMISe (UK)EGDT no benefit, and more costly

What changed? Not that Rivers was wrong for 2001 — but that 'usual care' caught up. The trio (ProCESS/ARISE/ProMISe) showed that the rigid protocol and its specific tools — mandatory central venous catheters, CVP targets, forced transfusion to Hct 30%, routine ScvO₂-guided dobutamine — are not required. What endured is the principle: recognise sepsis early, give timely fluids and antibiotics, start pressors early, and reassess perfusion repeatedly.

⚠️ Danger — CVP is dead as a resuscitation target

Central venous pressure does not predict fluid responsiveness and should not be used to decide whether to give more fluid. The post-EGDT era buried the rigid CVP 8–12 goal. Use dynamic measures of fluid responsiveness (passive leg raise, stroke-volume variation, fluid-challenge response) instead — and stop giving fluid when the patient is no longer fluid-responsive, however 'low' the CVP.

7 · MAP targets — SEPSISPAM revisited 🎯

The perfusion-pressure endpoint is a MAP ≥65 mmHg (Session 5). SEPSISPAM compared 65–70 vs 80–85 mmHg: no overall mortality difference, more atrial fibrillation at the higher target, but less renal replacement therapy in chronically hypertensive patients at 80–85. So the mantra: default MAP ≥65; individualise upward for chronic hypertension; do not push supranormal pressures in everyone.

8 · Putting the targets together 🧩

TargetWhat it measuresHow to use it
MAP ≥65Perfusion pressureNon-negotiable floor; individualise up in chronic HTN (SEPSISPAM)
Lactate clearanceGlobal hypoperfusion (with Type-B caveats)Aim for a downward trend, not zero; failure to clear = hunt for a source
CRT normalisationPeripheral/micro-perfusionNon-inferior to lactate (ANDROMEDA-SHOCK); gives less fluid; cross-checks Type-B lactate
ScvO₂/SvO₂Delivery vs extraction balanceLow = improve flow; a high value can be falsely reassuring
Urine output, mentationEnd-organ perfusionSimple, continuous clinical endpoints

No single number rules. Resuscitate to a convergence of endpoints — a perfused-looking patient (fast CRT, warm, making urine, clearing mentation) with an adequate MAP and a falling lactate — and be willing to stop fluid once the patient is no longer fluid-responsive.

☠️ M&M — the lactate that was chased to the ventilator

A 58-year-old man with septic shock was resuscitated well: by hour 4 his MAP was 70 on noradrenaline, his hands were warm, his CRT was under 2 seconds, and he was passing urine. But his lactate, having fallen from 6 to 2.8, then hovered at 2.5 and would not normalise. The team, fixated on 'clearing the lactate,' gave a further 4 litres of crystalloid over the next hours. The lactate barely moved — because it was now Type B, generated by his noradrenaline infusion and slow hepatic clearance — but his lungs did not tolerate the fluid: he developed florid pulmonary oedema, desaturated, and was intubated for fluid-overload respiratory failure that he had not needed. Lesson: once the patient is perfused (CRT normal, warm, urinating, MAP adequate), a stubborn low-level lactate is usually Type B, not under-resuscitation. Trust the fingertip over the number, target lactate clearance not normalisation, and stop giving fluid to a patient who is no longer fluid-responsive.

9 · Take-home 📌

  • Lactate is a marker of hypoperfusion (Type A) and a powerful mortality predictor — but it also rises for non-hypoxic (Type B) reasons: β₂-adrenergic aerobic glycolysis (including your catecholamines) and impaired hepatic clearance.
  • Target lactate CLEARANCE (a downward trend), not normalisation to zero; a ≥10–20% fall in 2 h is a reasonable goal. Failure to clear = hunt for an uncontrolled source.
  • CRT-guided resuscitation (ANDROMEDA-SHOCK) is non-inferior — possibly superior — to lactate clearance, gives less fluid, and avoids the Type-B trap.
  • ScvO₂/SvO₂ reflects delivery vs extraction — low means improve flow; a high value can be falsely reassuring due to mitochondrial/microcirculatory shunting.
  • Rigid protocolised EGDT is dead (ProCESS, ARISE, ProMISe) — but its principles (early recognition, timely fluids/antibiotics, early pressors, repeated reassessment) endure. CVP is not a fluid-responsiveness target.
  • MAP ≥65 is the pressure floor; individualise up in chronic hypertension (SEPSISPAM).
  • Resuscitate to a convergence of endpoints, and stop fluid when the patient is no longer fluid-responsive.

moderatorQs.q: Explain the difference between type A and type B lactate, and why it matters during resuscitation.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Type A lactate is hypoxic — tissue oxygen delivery fails, pyruvate is shunted to lactate; this dominates early septic shock and is a strong mortality predictor. Type B is non-hypoxic — lactate rises without tissue hypoxia, driven by β₂-adrenergic aerobic glycolysis (endogenous stress catecholamines and the adrenaline/noradrenaline you infuse) and by impaired hepatic clearance. It matters because a lactate that persists after the patient is well-perfused is often Type B — and interpreting it as ongoing hypoperfusion drives harmful fluid overload. That is why we target lactate clearance, not normalisation.

moderatorQs.q: What did ANDROMEDA-SHOCK teach us about capillary refill versus lactate as a resuscitation target?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: ANDROMEDA-SHOCK randomised septic shock patients to resuscitation guided by capillary refill time normalisation (checked every 30 minutes) versus lactate clearance. The CRT arm had no worse 28-day mortality (a non-significant trend toward lower mortality), less organ dysfunction at 72 hours, and patients received less fluid; a Bayesian re-analysis suggested a high probability of benefit. The lesson is that CRT — a direct, zero-cost measure of peripheral perfusion — is at least non-inferior to lactate, avoids the Type-B lactate trap, and encourages a more conservative fluid strategy.

moderatorQs.q: Why did the ProCESS, ARISE and ProMISe trials overturn Rivers' EGDT — and what survived?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Rivers' 2001 single-centre trial showed rigid Early Goal-Directed Therapy (CVP 8–12, MAP ≥65, ScvO₂ ≥70%, transfusion to Hct 30%, dobutamine) cut mortality dramatically. But ProCESS, ARISE and ProMISe — three large multicentre trials — each found protocolised EGDT gave no mortality benefit over contemporary usual care, at greater cost. What died is the rigid protocol and its mandatory tools (central lines for ScvO₂, CVP targets, forced transfusion). What survived is the principle: recognise sepsis early, give timely fluids and antibiotics, start vasopressors early, and reassess perfusion repeatedly. Notably, CVP is no longer a valid fluid-responsiveness target.

audienceQs.q: My patient looks perfused — warm, good urine output, CRT under 2 seconds — but the lactate is stuck at 2.4. Do I keep giving fluid?
audienceQs.answerHTML: No. A well-perfused patient — fast CRT, warm peripheries, making urine, adequate MAP — with a stubborn low-level lactate almost always has a Type B lactate: β₂-adrenergic aerobic glycolysis from the stress response and any catecholamine infusion, plus sluggish hepatic clearance. Target lactate clearance (a downward trend), not normalisation to zero, and trust the perfusion signs over the number. Pushing more fluid into a patient who is no longer fluid-responsive risks pulmonary oedema and worse outcomes.

audienceQs.q: Should I still be using CVP to decide whether to give more fluid?
audienceQs.answerHTML: No — CVP does not predict fluid responsiveness and was abandoned as a resuscitation target after the EGDT trials. Use dynamic measures instead: a passive leg raise, stroke-volume variation, or the response to a small fluid challenge. Give fluid only while the patient is genuinely fluid-responsive, and stop once they are not — regardless of what the CVP reads.

audienceQs.q: What is a normal capillary refill time and how should I be measuring it consistently?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Apply firm pressure to the fingertip or nail bed for a few seconds, release, and time the return of colour — greater than 3 seconds is abnormal. In ANDROMEDA-SHOCK it was standardised and rechecked every 30 minutes during active resuscitation. Do it on a warm limb in consistent lighting, ideally the same finger each time, so the trend is reliable. A normalising CRT in a warm, urinating patient is a strong sign of restored peripheral perfusion.
